title: Wheat and Millet Meet in the Mountains
text: Long before 3000 BCE, farmers in western Asia grew wheat while farmers in China grew broomcorn millet. At Begash, a herders' camp in the highland steppe of eastern Kazakhstan, archaeologists found both grains together, in a cremation burial from the camp's earliest phase. They are among the earliest crops known to have reached the mountains of Inner Asia, carried along herders' networks.

source.name: Antiquity (Cambridge Core): Earliest direct evidence for broomcorn millet and wheat in the central Eurasian steppe region

source2.name: Proceedings of the Royal Society B (PMC): Early agriculture and crop transmission among Bronze Age mobile pastoralists of Central Eurasia

title: A Steppe King and Queen in Gold
text: In Tuva's 'Valley of the Kings', every burial mound dug before had been robbed in ancient times, but Arzhan-2 held an untouched grave. A man and a woman lay in a larch-wood chamber, their clothes sewn with some 5,000 tiny gold cats. He wore a massive gold torque covered in deer, boars, camels, snow leopards and wolves, and carried weapons of iron, then a new metal.

source.name: State Hermitage Museum: The discovery of an outstanding 'royal' burial of the Scythian period in Tuva

source2.name: Radiocarbon (Cambridge Core): Chronology of key barrows of the Scythian period in Tuva (Arzhan-1 and Arzhan-2)

title: The Polymath From Beyond the Oxus
text: Al-Biruni was born in Khwarezm, beyond the Oxus River, and once wrote in a poem that he did not even know his own father. He became perhaps the most original polymath of the Islamic world, writing 146 titles, almost half on astronomy and mathematics. His great book on India recorded its science, religion and customs, but only 22 of his works survive.

title: Gravestones That Named the Plague
text: In the Chüy Valley near Lake Issyk-Kul lived trading communities whose gravestones, dated 1338–1339, give 'pestilence' as the cause of death. Scientists recovered DNA of the plague bacterium from people buried there. The strain sits at the root of the family of plague strains linked to the Black Death, pointing to an origin in the Tian Shan region, where related strains still live in marmots.

source.name: Nature (PMC): The source of the Black Death in fourteenth-century central Eurasia

title: Timur's Giant Dome for a Sufi Master
text: Khoja Ahmed Yasawi was a distinguished Sufi master of the 12th century. In 1389 Timur began a vast mausoleum for him, 38.7 metres tall, and is said to have joined in the building work himself. Its dome is the largest in Central Asia. When Timur died in 1405, the main entrance was left unfinished, and the ideas tested here were reused in Samarkand.

source.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre: Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi

title: The Breakaway That Made the Kazakhs
place: Chu and Talas rivers, Zhambyl Region, Kazakhstan
text: Around 1465, two leaders, Karay and Jani Beg, led some 200,000 unhappy subjects of the Uzbek khan Abu'l-Khayr into Mughulistan. Its khan of Mughulistan settled them between the Chu and Talas rivers. People called them the Kazakh, 'independent' or 'vagabond', Uzbeks. They became more nomadic than the Uzbeks and soon ruled almost the entire steppe.

title: The Great Disaster on the Steppe
text: In 1723 the Dzungars, western Mongols led by Tsewang Rabtan, launched a devastating invasion of the eastern Kazakh lands. Oddly, they were helped by Swedish officers, prisoners captured by Russia at the Battle of Poltava who had drifted this far east. Kazakhs still remember it as the 'Great Disaster', and it pushed some of them to seek Russian protection.

title: Shots at the Lena Gold Mines
text: At the Lena gold mines in Siberia, a file of workers about three thousand strong marched out of the deforested hills toward a company settlement on the Bodaibo River. A company of soldiers stood waiting beyond a bridge. Troops killed some 200 workers, and the massacre revived the workers' movement, with strikes and demonstrations breaking out in many of Russia's biggest cities.

source.name: Slavic Review (Cambridge Core): The Ninth Circle: The Lena Goldfield Workers and the Massacre of 4 April 1912

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Russia – The last years of tsardom

title: The 1916 Revolt and Flight
text: In the middle of World War I, Russia decided to draft Central Asians as unarmed workers to dig trenches and build fortifications. Many Kyrgyz and Kazakhs refused and rose in open revolt. The uprising was met with brutal, prolonged repression, and after it was crushed many Kyrgyz and Kazakhs fled across the mountains to Xinjiang in China.

source2.name: Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty: Convoy in Kyrgyzstan commemorates 1916 anti-Russia revolt

title: Hujum: The Campaign Against the Veil
text: On International Women's Day 1927, activists in Tashkent launched the hujum, a campaign to end the paranja, the head-to-toe veil worn by urban Muslim women. Many women publicly burned their veils, but then quietly wore them again or swapped them for shawls. In the first years thousands of women were attacked and hundreds killed, often by their own male relatives.

source.name: Davis Center, Harvard University: The Thorny Road to Emancipation: Women in Soviet Central Asia

title: The Coldest Village in the North
text: On 6 February 1933 the village of Oymyakon in eastern Siberia, 800 metres up, recorded −67.8°C (−90°F), the World Meteorological Organization's record low for Asia. Verkhoyansk had logged similar cold in 1892, but with less accurate spirit thermometers. Most Russian climatologists consider Oymyakon the coldest place in the Northern Hemisphere.

source.name: World Meteorological Organization: WMO Region II (Asia) – Lowest Temperature

title: The Khan Whose Skull Became a Cup
text: By 1500 the Uzbek leader Muhammad Shaybani had made himself master of Samarkand, and he went on to take Herat in 1507. In 1510 the Iranian shah Ismail I ambushed his army near Merv, beating 28,000 Uzbeks with only 17,000 Iranians. Shaybani was killed trying to escape, and Ismail had his skull made into a jewelled drinking goblet.

source2.name: Encyclopaedia Britannica: History of Central Asia – Timur and the Uzbeks (Denis Sinor et al.)

title: The White Huns Beat Persia
text: The Hephthalites, or White Huns, entered Bactria early in the 5th century. A Byzantine writer said they lived in towns rather than as nomads, and buried nobles in mounds together with their companions. The Persian king Peroz fought them three times, all disastrously; in the last, in 484, he charged to his death into a hidden ditch with all his cavalry.

title: The Hill of Gold
place: Tillya Tepe, near Sheberghan, Jowzjan, Afghanistan
text: At Tillya Tepe in northern Afghanistan, a nomad chieftain and five women were buried wearing crowns, swords and clothes covered in tiny gold pieces, many set with turquoise and garnets. Their jewellery blends nomadic, Greek, Indian and Chinese imagery. Hidden in a Kabul bank vault through 25 years of war, the hoard was found intact in 2003.

source.name: Metropolitan Museum of Art: Afghanistan's Dazzling National Treasures, Hidden for 25 Years
